case_info.scenario: A large oral mass was noted at time of delivery in a female neonate at gestational age of 39 weeks. Primary symptom was difficulty feeding without notable respiratory distress. Prenatal history included maternal herpes simplex virus, well controlled with valacyclovir. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck with and without contrast was obtained showing a 3-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the posterior aspect of the tongue, abutting the inferior surface of the uvula with mild T1 hypointensity. On examination, a tan lobulated-appearing mass was noted occupying nearly all of the oral cavity and was adherent to the tongue posteriorly. No connection was noted to soft or hard palate, buccal mucosa, tonsillar fossae, or alveolar ridges. Surgical excision was performed on day 6 of life. The mass was noted to be attached just anteriorly to the dorsal lingual papillae with a wide base and was excised from the underlying tongue using cautery along with a cuff of lingual tissue (Figure 1). Direct laryngoscopy after removal of the mass revealed a grade I view with no other lesions present. Primary suture closure was accomplished without difficulty. The final specimen measured 3.5 cm anterior to posterior, 2.3 cm medial to lateral, and 1.1 cm in average thickness. The internal tissue was yellow-tan, fatty, and interdigitating with the underlying musculature.

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

Direct laryngoscopy after removal of the mass revealed a grade I view with no other lesions present. Primary suture closure was accomplished without difficulty. The final specimen measured 3.5 cm anterior to posterior, 2.3 cm medial to lateral, and 1.1 cm in average thickness. [NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.

       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task

       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's

   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a

       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck with and without contrast was obtained showing a 3-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the posterior aspect of the tongue, abutting the inferior surface of the uvula with mild T1 hypointensity. On examination, a tan lobulated-appearing mass was noted occupying nearly all of the oral cavity and was adherent to the tongue posteriorly. No connection was noted to soft or hard palate, buccal mucosa, tonsillar fossae, or alveolar ridges. Surgical excision was performed on day 6 of life. The mass was noted to be attached just anteriorly to the dorsal lingual papillae with a wide base and was excised from the underlying tongue using cautery along with a cuff of lingual tissue (Figure 1). Direct laryngoscopy after removal of the mass revealed a grade I view with no other lesions present. Primary suture closure was accomplished without difficulty. The final specimen measured 3.5 cm anterior to posterior, 2.3 cm medial to lateral, and 1.1 cm in average thickness. The internal tissue was yellow-tan, fatty, and interdigitating with the underlying musculature.

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."

case_info.explanation: On microscopic evaluation, the specimen consisted of glioneuronal tissue showing both neurons positive for NeuN1 and glial cells positive for glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in a fibrotic background. CD57 was previously well utilized for glial heterotopia, but GFAP has replaced this stain in most institutions. The neuronal component showed focal forms with eosinophilic cytoplasm and a peripherally positioned, flattened nucleus. The specimen had 2 mitotic figures per 10 high-powered fields, structures consistent with choroid plexus, and negative HMB45 staining. HMB45 is useful to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy, as other melanoma markers are typically negative. The pigmented macrophages are highlighted by CD68, and a second stain is needed to rule out melanotic neuroectodermal tumor of infancy. While rare, it is found in the oral cavity. CD68 staining showed marked increase in macrophages. Granular cell tumor is a mimic of glial heterotopia; this neuroectodermal tumor is differentiated by CD68, which draws attention to cytoplasmic lysosomal granules, negative in this tumor. Ki-67 index was high at 15% to 20%. This was consistent with diagnosis of glial heterotopia (Figure 2). Glial heterotopia is a congenital, nonhereditary malformation of infants that represents benign cerebral tissue of extracranial sites. It most frequently occurs in the nasal area but rarely can present at other sites of the head and neck, including oral cavity, middle ear, tonsillar fossa, and orbit.1,2It is considered benign, although rare cases of malignant transformation have been reported. It is estimated to occur in 20 000 to 40 000 live births; more frequently in males at an approximate 3:2 ratio. Most cases are diagnosed by age 3 years.3 Glial cells are normally located in the central nervous system and serve as neuronal support cells. The development of glial heterotopia is embryologically similar to encephaloceles or dermoid cysts.4There are many proposed mechanisms, including encephalocele that loses intracranial connection, displacement of neuroectodermal cells during early embryogenesis, or glial cell migration from the olfactory bulb. Glial heterotopia lesions consist of mature astrocytes and glial fibers embedded in a fibrovascular stroma, often with elements of ependymal lined structures including choroid plexus, as in the present case.5,6 Workup for these lesions should include imaging such as ultrasonography, computed tomography, or MRI to rule out intracranial extent or skull base defects prior to intervention.3,7MRI and computed tomography cannot distinguish a glial heterotopic lesion from other common midline masses of the head and neck, including thyroglossal duct cyst, teratoma, and lymphatic malformations.6Biopsy can be considered after ruling out intracranial extent, especially in older patients to rule out malignancy.4Surgical resection is generally recommended, especially in the setting of functional complications including airway distress, dysphagia, or failure to thrive.4,5Early surgical intervention is recommended in the case of rapid growth. Recurrence is not uncommon, at a reported rate of 4% to 15%. This is more common in the first few weeks after surgical resection.4Complete resection with histologically clear margins and a follow-up period of at least 12 months is recommended. Repeat MRI can be considered in cases of uncertain recurrence.4There is an overall lack of long-term outcome data for these patients.4 Congenital epulis is another rare congenital phenomenon of the oral cavity, generally located on the alveolar ridge but can rarely present on the tongue. Management for these lesions includes surgical excision, and diagnosis is made on pathological examination showing large sheets of typical polygonal granular cells without nuclear atypia and no particular cellular arrangement.8Lymphatic malformations show anastomosing lymphatic and venous channels on histology.9Lingual thyroid has similar histologic features to normal thyroid tissue, and generally arises at the foramen cecum.10

[Case]
A large oral mass was noted at time of delivery in a female neonate at gestational age of 39 weeks. Primary symptom was difficulty feeding without notable respiratory distress. Prenatal history included maternal herpes simplex virus, well controlled with valacyclovir. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the neck with and without contrast was obtained showing a 3-cm heterogeneously enhancing mass arising from the posterior aspect of the tongue, abutting the inferior surface of the uvula with mild T1 hypointensity. On examination, a tan lobulated-appearing mass was noted occupying nearly all of the oral cavity and was adherent to the tongue posteriorly. No connection was noted to soft or hard palate, buccal mucosa, tonsillar fossae, or alveolar ridges. Surgical excision was performed on day 6 of life. The mass was noted to be attached just anteriorly to the dorsal lingual papillae with a wide base and was excised from the underlying tongue using cautery along with a cuff of lingual tissue (Figure 1). Direct laryngoscopy after removal of the mass revealed a grade I view with no other lesions present. Primary suture closure was accomplished without difficulty. The final specimen measured 3.5 cm anterior to posterior, 2.3 cm medial to lateral, and 1.1 cm in average thickness. The internal tissue was yellow-tan, fatty, and interdigitating with the underlying musculature.
